name: Akuntsú
confidence_why: Aragon's 2014 reference grammar, the only full description of Akuntsú, states that stress falls unpredictably on the final or penultimate syllable and proposes lexical stress on the strength of a few minimal pairs, and her 2008 thesis gives the same two-syllable window, so the reading is uncontested but rests on a single fieldworker who calls her own analysis tentative.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each lexical word carries one primary stress on either its final or its penultimate syllable; which of the two is not predictable from syllable weight or from morphology (affixes count like root syllables), and (near-)minimal pairs such as /bago/ [ˈbago] 'dry' vs. [baˈgo] 'ant sp.' and /kʷiɾi/ [kʷiˈɾi] 'açaí' vs. [ˈkʷiɾi] 'day/clean/empty' point to lexically specified (phonemic) stress confined to a right-edge two-syllable window. No lexical word of four or more syllables was found with final stress. The chapter summary (p. 117) labels the language iambic, with primary stress on the right-most foot of a word or phrase, and §3.2.1 (p. 119) says a phonological word must bear a foot at its right edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, described for compounds and phonological phrases: 'the rightmost component of the compound is assigned the strongest (primary) stress, and stress on the other component is reduced (secondary)' (§2.4.5 p. 105, e.g. /oɾoɾo/ + /pe/ → [oˌɾoɾoˈpɛ] 'clothes'); likewise in phrases the primary stress goes on the right-most word and earlier words are reduced to secondary (e.g. [aˌpaɾaˈka] '(he/she) eats bananas', p. 112; §3.2.1 p. 119).
new_statements.exceptions: Proclitics (dependent personal pronouns) are integrated into the phonological word and shift stress: /kado/ [kaˈɾo] 'necklace' → /o=kado/ [uˈkaɾo] 'my necklace' (§2.4.4 p. 104, ex. 2.85-2.86, 2.95); suffixes and prefixes do not affect the pattern (they count like root syllables). Verbs are never pronounced in isolation, so verbal stress interacts with adjacent function words (p. 108). In discourse, when two words combine and the resulting clause is 'uneven', stress falls on the penultimate (ex. 2.97c, p. 113). Content words are more prominent than function words, which are often reduced (p. 113). The author calls the analysis 'the first tentative analysis of stress assignment in Akuntsú; therefore there is room for further investigation' (p. 108).
new_statements.identity_note: Aragon 2014 describes Akuntsú as spoken by its last few speakers in the Rio Omerê area, Rondônia, Brazil (Tuparían subfamily of Tupían); no dialects are distinguished, so no identity issue. The grammar's title on the PDF is 'A Grammar of Akuntsú, a Tupían Language' (the citation in the target list reads 'A Descriptive Grammar of Akuntsú'); same author, year, institution and content, so it is the listed item.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the listed works (only one). Two points worth recording. (1) Aragon's own earlier MA thesis (Aragon 2008, UnB, already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass, not in this works list) says at §2.7 p. 79 and in the chapter summary p. 81 that 'o acento na língua Akuntsú pode ocorrer na última e na penúltima sílaba, aparentemente sem caráter distintivo' (stress can fall on the last or penultimate syllable, apparently without distinctive character); the 2014 grammar keeps the final/penultimate window but moves toward lexical (phonemic) stress on the strength of near-minimal pairs, while conceding the pairs 'may be not so convincing'. So the two Aragon works agree on placement (final or penultimate) but differ on whether the choice is contrastive. (2) Within the 2014 grammar there is a mild internal tension: §2.5.2 (p. 111) states placement within the two-syllable window is 'unpredictable', while the chapter summary (p. 117) and §3.2.1 (p. 119) describe the language as 'iambic' with primary stress on the right-most foot; the author flags the whole analysis as tentative.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated pages in the held 2014 dissertation, which is the fullest and only substantial description of Akuntsú prosody (reference grammar with acoustic measurements, by the sole fieldworker). The earlier 2008 MA thesis (downloaded to gives the same final/penult window and defers analysis to future work. Coding 'lexical, right-edge two-syllable window, weight-insensitive' matches the author's explicit statements; the only caveat worth carrying in a caution field is that the author herself calls the analysis tentative and elsewhere (§2.4.5 p.105, §2.6 p.117) characterises the language as iambic with final stress as the majority pattern and no 4+-syllable word attested with final stress — a 'final-default with lexical penult' reading is possible but the source's own word is 'unpredictable', so no reclassification is warrant
